status: Draft from the mishnah, R. Kulp and Kehati. Chapters 1-6 form a unit about damage caused by one's property or act.

principles.t: Four primary causes of injury: the ox, the pit, the crop-destroying beast and fire. Each is in the Torah, and each has a feature the others lack.
What I am bound to guard, if I did not guard it, I have prepared (hichsharti) its damage, even if only partly.
Damages are paid only for property that is not sacred, belongs to Jews, is owned, and is damaged outside the damager's own domain and the domain shared by both.
Damages are assessed in money before a court of experts on the evidence of free Jewish witnesses. Women are included.
A harmless animal (tam) pays half damages from its own body; an attested danger (mu'ad) pays full damages from the best property.

terms.def: The four basic categories of damage in the Torah: ox, pit, crop-destroying beast and fire.
An animal not yet an attested danger for a given damage. Its owner pays half damages from the animal's own value.
An agent (or an animal that has been warned) whose way is to damage. Its owner pays full damages from the best property. A human being is always one.

terms.term: from the best of his land
terms.def: The payment for full damages comes from the best of the payer's land.

debates.title: What are the four primary causes?
debates.a: Rav: the mishnah names the main kinds of damage in the Torah.
debates.b: Shmuel: it names only four kinds of property damage that are attested dangers from the start (foot, tooth, pit, fire). Kehati follows Shmuel.

debates.title: Do tame wild animals count as attested dangers?
debates.a: The first view: the wolf, lion, bear, leopard, panther and snake are attested dangers.
debates.b: Rabbi Eliezer: tame ones are not, but the snake always is. The halakha does not follow him.
